source.title_on_document: How and for Whom Using Generative AI Affects Creativity: A Field Experiment

supplement.holds: Supplemental Tables S1-S4 (item-level analyses of cognitive job resources), results without control variables (Supplemental Table S5 Model 4 for usefulness; footnote 2 cites Supplemental Materials S4 for multilevel analyses without controls), and Supplemental Sections S6-S8 (robustness tests of the metacognitive-strategies moderation and practical significance).

paper_design_summary: 250 nonmanagerial employees of a technology consulting firm in China were randomly assigned on August 7, 2023 to receive ChatGPT accounts (via the firm's OpenAI API interface) or no access. About a week later (August 15), direct supervisors rated each employee's creative performance over the week, and two external raters scored the novelty and usefulness of each employee's written answer (at least 70 Chinese characters) to a question on protecting employee privacy. The paper also tests self-reported cognitive job resources as mediator and metacognitive strategies as moderator.

studies.label: Field experiment at a Chinese technology consulting firm (ChatGPT access vs. none)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Access to ChatGPT accounts (treatment) versus no ChatGPT access (control)
assignment.quote: Next, on August 7, 2023, participants were randomly assigned to either the treatment or control group using a random number generator. Employees in the treatment group received ChatGPT accounts with usage examples
assignment.locator: printed pp. 4-5 (PDF pp. 5-6), Method, Participants and Procedure
assignment.prereg_locator: printed p. 4 (PDF p. 5), Method, Transparency and Openness: "This study is not preregistered."

arms.name: LLM assistance condition
arms.description: Received ChatGPT accounts with usage examples, for personal use only; told ChatGPT was intended to assist, not replace, their roles. Logs show every treated employee used ChatGPT (M = 33.72 uses, SD = 8.17).

arms.name: Control condition
arms.description: No ChatGPT access; control employees reported no ChatGPT usage.

participants.exclusions: 286 eligible employees were invited; 36 did not participate because of business travel and illness, giving a final sample of 250 before random assignment. All analyses report N = 250 (Tables 1 and 3). Per-arm counts are not printed; Table 1 gives a mean of 0.50 for the condition dummy.
participants.who: Nonmanagerial employees in technology, sales/consulting, and administration departments of a technology consulting firm (excluding those already experimenting with the ChatGPT API); 64.8% male, mean age 29.59 (SD 4.37); nested within 30 supervisors and 3 departments.
participants.quote: Due to business travel and illnesses, 36 employees did not participate, resulting in a final sample of 250 employees.
participants.locator: printed p. 4 (PDF p. 5), Participants and Procedure; printed p. 5 (PDF p. 6), Results

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT via the firm's OpenAI API-based interface (model version not stated)
ai_tool.how_used: Treated employees got ChatGPT accounts with usage examples and used them freely in their work for about a week (August 7 to August 15, 2023). Self-reported usage frequency M = 4.14 (SD 0.81) on a 1-5 scale; usage logs M = 33.72 (SD 8.17).

task.description: Ordinary consulting work over one week, rated by supervisors for general creative performance; plus a written idea-generation prompt in the second survey (suggestions for protecting employee privacy in the digital workplace, at least 70 Chinese characters) scored by external raters.
task.duration: About one week of access (assignment August 7, 2023; second survey and ratings from August 15, 2023)

outcomes.name: Creativity (supervisor rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Direct supervisors rated each employee's general creative performance over the week on Zhou and George's (2001) creativity scale (1-5, alpha = .97); supervisors approached only at the end of the experiment and blind to hypotheses and design. A rating of work performance rather than of one specified output. Variants: with controls (Table 3 Model 2), with mediator (Model 5, gamma = 0.71), without controls in supplement.
outcomes.delay: Rated at the end of the roughly one-week access period (assignment August 7; ratings after August 15, 2023)

contrasts.reported: Table 2: control M = 3.05, SD = 1.09; LLM assistance M = 4.14, SD = 0.58; p value of t-test = .000; Cohen's d = 1.25 (arm ns not printed; N = 250 total). Table 3 Model 2 (multilevel, with controls): gamma = 0.84, SE = 0.10, p < .001.
contrasts.locator: printed p. 7 (PDF p. 8), Table 2; printed p. 9 (PDF p. 10), Table 3 Model 2; printed p. 5 (PDF p. 6), Results

outcomes.name: Novelty (external raters' rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two external raters, blind to hypotheses and design, independently scored the novelty of each employee's written answer on privacy protection using the consensual assessment technique (1-5); ICC = .78. The paper does not describe the raters' expertise. Variants: with controls (Table 3 Model 3), with mediator (Model 6, gamma = 0.17), without controls in supplement.
outcomes.delay: Written in the second survey on August 15, 2023, about 8 days after assignment

contrasts.reported: Table 2: control M = 2.78, SD = 0.96; LLM assistance M = 3.11, SD = 0.95; p value of t-test = .006; Cohen's d = 0.35 (arm ns not printed; N = 250 total). Table 3 Model 3 (multilevel, with controls): gamma = 0.25, SE = 0.13, p = .049.
contrasts.locator: printed p. 7 (PDF p. 8), Table 2; printed p. 9 (PDF p. 10), Table 3 Model 3; printed p. 5 (PDF p. 6), Results

outcomes.name: Usefulness (external raters' rating)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two external raters independently scored the usefulness of each employee's written answer on privacy protection (consensual assessment technique, 1-5); ICC = .69. Variants: with controls (Table 3 Model 4, not significant), without controls (Supplemental Table S5 Model 4), with mediator (Model 7, gamma = 0.02).
outcomes.delay: Written in the second survey on August 15, 2023, about 8 days after assignment

contrasts.reported: Table 2: control M = 2.87, SD = 0.82; LLM assistance M = 3.15, SD = 0.89; p value of t-test = .010; Cohen's d = 0.33 (arm ns not printed; N = 250 total). Table 3 Model 4 (multilevel, with controls): gamma = 0.17, SE = 0.11, p = .136; without controls (Supplemental Table S5 Model 4): gamma = 0.28, SE = 0.11, p = .009.

company_involvement.description: No AI developer involvement stated. The field-site firm (a Chinese technology consulting firm) had built an API-based ChatGPT interface and hosted the experiment; the authors exploited that rollout. The firm told treated employees ChatGPT was meant to assist, not replace, their roles.
company_involvement.locator: printed pp. 4-5 (PDF pp. 5-6), Empirical Setting; Participants and Procedure

eligibility.reason: Employees were individually randomized to ChatGPT access or none (printed pp. 4-5, PDF pp. 5-6); 250 people analyzed (Tables 1-3); creativity rated by supervisors and novelty and usefulness of a written idea rated by two external raters (printed p. 5, PDF p. 6). The supervisor measure rates general creative performance over the week rather than one output; the external-rater measures score a specific written response.

one_line_finding: ChatGPT access for one week raised supervisor-rated creativity (4.14 vs. 3.05, d = 1.25) and external-rater novelty (3.11 vs. 2.78, d = 0.35) and usefulness (3.15 vs. 2.87, d = 0.33) of 250 consulting-firm employees (Table 2, printed p. 7); with controls, usefulness is not significant (Table 3 Model 4, p = .136).
open_questions: The paper does not say whether treated employees could use ChatGPT while writing the privacy-protection answer in the second survey; I coded AI as available because accounts were active during the period, but this is not stated.
Per-arm sample sizes are not printed (only N = 250 and a condition mean of 0.50 in Table 1).
It is not stated whether supervisors knew which employees had ChatGPT; the paper says only that they were blind to hypotheses and experimental design.
External raters' expertise is not described, so the measure code (human_raters vs. expert_raters) is uncertain.
Footnote 2 refers to multilevel analyses without controls in Supplemental Materials S4, while the text cites Supplemental Table S5 Model 4; the supplement is not on file.
notes: Data are not public (confidentiality agreement with the firm; available on request); analyses in Stata 16; ethics protocol Renmin University #2023R19 (printed p. 4). Multilevel models nest employees in 30 supervisors in 3 departments, with variance components at Levels 1-3 (Table 3). Not listed as outcomes: cognitive job resources (self-reported mediator: control 3.38 vs. LLM 4.15, d = 0.92, Table 2) and metacognitive strategies (self-reported moderator). Moderated mediation: conditional indirect effects at high metacognitive strategies were significant for creativity 0.23 [0.099, 0.375], novelty 0.16 [0.008, 0.328], and usefulness 0.22 [0.083, 0.376], and nonsignificant at low levels (printed p. 6). The paper speculates about long-run downsides of reliance on LLMs (printed pp. 10-11) but measures no after-AI outcome; the lead in candidates.json about lower later independent creativity is not supported by this document.
